title: The lamp in a windless place
hook: the Gita's picture of a settled mind is a flame that doesn't flicker
carry: the settled mind: a lamp out of the wind

segments.voice: Yesterday, asana: a clean place, a firm seat, the mind on God. Today, what happens once you're sitting there.
screen: `ASANA — A CLEAN PLACE, A FIRM SEAT.`

segments.voice: Light a small oil lamp, a diya, the kind lit at a home shrine, and set it by an open window. Watch it. The flame bends, leans, jumps, nearly goes out, flares back. Every breath of air pushes it around. Now carry it into an inner room and shut the door. The flame straightens. It stands tall and still, so still it almost looks painted. Same lamp. Same oil. The only difference is the wind. The Gita, chapter six, uses that picture for the mind.
screen: `A LAMP BY AN OPEN WINDOW.` → `SHUT THE DOOR.` → `THE FLAME STANDS STILL.`

segments.voice: Verse nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, that is the picture of the yogi whose mind is held, practicing union with the self. The Sanskrit is simple: dipa, the lamp; nivata, where there's no wind. Notice the lamp is still burning. A settled mind hasn't gone out. It's fully lit, just not being pushed around. That's the Hindu teaching of yoga in one picture: not an empty mind, a steady one, resting in the self. Then the verses say what that stillness opens onto. Where the mind comes to rest, seeing the self by the self, a person is content in the self. They know a joy beyond the senses, and once settled there, even heavy sorrow doesn't shake them. Then a definition I like a lot, from verse twenty-three: yoga is the unhooking from union with sorrow. Yoga is often heard as joining. Here it's also an unjoining. Now the practical part. Verse twenty-five: little by little, let the mind grow still. Shanaih shanaih: slowly, slowly. And verse twenty-six gives the method in one sentence: wherever the restless mind wanders off, draw it back from there and bring it under the self. Not never wandering. Coming back. Your day is an open window: every buzz, every tab, a gust. You won't stop the wind. Notice the lean, and shut the door again.
screen: `A LAMP THAT DOES NOT FLICKER.` · `STILL, AND FULLY LIT.` · `UNHOOKED FROM SORROW.` · `SLOWLY, SLOWLY. COME BACK.` · then, large: `THE LAMP IN A WINDLESS PLACE.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle or a small lamp and set it where the air is still; if not, picture one just in front of you. Watch the flame. Each time a thought blows in, notice the mind lean, then gently bring it back to the flame, without being annoyed at the wind. Verse twenty-six expects it: the practice is the returning, slowly, slowly, as many times as it takes.
Dipa. Lamp. Gita six, nineteen: as a lamp in a windless place does not flicker, so is the settled mind, fully lit and still.
Your line: the settled mind, a lamp out of the wind. Fully lit, and not pushed around. Day one hundred eighty, done.

howItsDone: Hindus often light a lamp (diya) at the home shrine morning or evening, and some meditate by gazing at a steady flame; Gita 6.19's windless lamp is a classic image of the settled mind.

original.note: Sanskrit: dipa, lamp; the same root as diya and Diwali (dipavali, a row of lamps).

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means an empty mind.
what it means: a mind like a lamp out of the wind: fully lit, not flickering, brought back whenever it wanders.
what a scholar hears: 6.19 reads 'yatha dipo nivata-stho nengate', a lamp standing where no wind is doesn't waver; 6.23 defines yoga as 'duhkha-samyoga-viyoga', a play on joining and unjoining.
